summary: This RFC reproduces an addendum to the ISO Network Service Definition (ISO 8348) that defines the abstract syntax and meaning of a Network Address, the address used in connection-mode and connectionless network services.

eli5.summary: It describes how another group's networks write down addresses, like the exact rules for how a full postal address is laid out.

questions: what is the iso network address format
subtitle: How the ISO standard defines network-layer addresses so any computer in the world can be uniquely identified.

tldr.problem: As computer networks grew more interconnected across the world, there was no agreed-upon way to write down a network address that would unambiguously identify any computer on any network, and no standard for who gets to assign these addresses.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 941 reproduces the ISO 8348 addendum that defines NSAP (Network Service Access Point) addresses using a hierarchical structure: an Initial Domain Part (IDP) that identifies an address authority, and a Domain-Specific Part (DSP) that the authority assigns as it chooses. Different IDI formats (X.121, ISO DCC, E.164 phone numbers, etc.) cover different real-world numbering systems.
tldr.outcome: This created a global addressing hierarchy that could grow without centralized bottleneck: each authority controls its own subdomain, higher authorities control how subdomains are created, and any NSAP can be globally identified. The framework was adopted by ISO standards bodies but was eventually displaced by IPv4 and IPv6 in the Internet.

facts.value: 7 (X.121, ISO DCC, F.69, E.163, E.164, ISO 6523-ICD, Local)

facts.value: 4 (binary octets, decimal digits, ISO 646 characters, national characters)

today: RFC 941 is Informational and remains a historical record of ISO's OSI addressing architecture. While ISO NSAP addressing was carefully designed and theoretically sound, it was displaced in practice by IPv4 and IPv6. Today's Internet uses 32-bit IPv4 or 128-bit IPv6 addresses instead of the variable-length hierarchical NSAP format.

sections.title: NSAP Addressing Standard
sections.content:
RFC 941 is a reproduction of ISO/DP 8348/DAD2 (a Draft Proposed Addendum to the ISO 8348 Network Service Definition) from October 1984, prepared by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) Technical Committee 97, Subcommittee 6. This addendum defines the abstract semantics and concrete syntax for Network Service Access Point (NSAP) addresses, the addresses used in the OSI network layer when two systems communicate.

An NSAP address uniquely identifies a point where an application can access network services. The same address format works for both connection-oriented and connectionless network services, and RFC 941 provides the foundation for how addresses are allocated and interpreted globally.
sections.eli5: This document explains the official international rules for writing down network addresses so that any computer anywhere in the world can be found.

sections.title: Addressing Concepts
sections.content:
RFC 941 distinguishes three types of network addresses. A subnetwork address identifies a point of attachment to a specific real network (like a DTE/DCE interface to a public data network). An NSAP address identifies a service access point to the OSI network service, used in primitives like N-CONNECT. A network protocol address information (NPAI) is the encoding of an NSAP address within a protocol message.

The standard also introduces the concept of domains: a domain is a region where identifiers of the same type are unambiguous. There is a global network addressing domain (all NSAPs worldwide) and subdomains within it. Each domain has an authority that ensures uniqueness: the authority assigns identifiers and may create further subdomains, delegating to sub-authorities.
sections.eli5: An address has three parts: which network you are on, who is in charge of that area, and your unique number in that area.

sections.title: Hierarchical Address Structure
sections.content:
NSAP addresses follow a hierarchical structure based on domains and subdomains, much like a postal system. At any level, an initial part of the address unambiguously identifies a subdomain, and the rest is allocated by the subdomain's authority to identify either a lower subdomain or a service access point within the subdomain.

This hierarchy allows the addressing system to grow without bottleneck. The root authority (ISO and CCITT jointly) defines initial domain parts; each IDI format (like X.121 or ISO DCC) represents a different branch. Organizations designated as addressing authorities control their branch and can delegate to sub-authorities. The structure is illustrated via inverted tree diagrams and domain diagrams in the RFC.

Critically, route independence is maintained: Network Service users cannot derive routing information from an NSAP address, so the address structure does not constrain the actual path packets take through the network.
sections.eli5: The whole world is divided into regions, regions into sub-regions, and each sub-region into neighborhoods, with one person in charge of each level, checking that no two addresses are the same.

sections.title: Address Format and Components
sections.content:
An NSAP address consists of two main parts: the Initial Domain Part (IDP) and the Domain-Specific Part (DSP). The IDP itself has two components: the Authority and Format Identifier (AFI) and the Initial Domain Identifier (IDI).

The AFI is a two-digit value (0 to 99) that specifies (a) the format of the IDI, (b) the authority responsible for allocating IDI values, and (c) the syntax of the DSP (decimal digits, binary octets, ISO 646 characters, or national characters). The IDI is a variable-length identifier (different formats: X.121 up to 14 digits, ISO DCC 3 digits, F.69 telex up to 8 digits, E.163 PSTN up to 12 digits, E.164 ISDN up to 15 digits, ISO 6523-ICD 4 digits, or Local null) that identifies which authority allocates the DSP.

The DSP contains the actual address within the subdomain identified by the IDI. Its syntax and meaning are determined entirely by the authority identified by the IDI. Maximum lengths and syntaxes are defined for each IDI format, allowing authorities to allocate up to 38 decimal digits for Local format or 15 binary octets for the DSP.
sections.eli5: An address is like a library call number: the first part says what country the book is in, the next part says who takes care of that country's books, and the rest is the book's unique number in that country.

sections.title: IDI Format Options
sections.content:
The standard defines seven IDI formats, each tying NSAP addressing to an existing real-world numbering system. X.121 uses CCITT's international data network numbering plan (up to 14 digits). ISO DCC uses a 3-digit Data Country Code allocated to ISO member countries, allowing geographically-based address allocation. F.69 uses telex destination codes. E.163 uses public switched telephone network (PSTN) country codes and numbers. E.164 uses ISDN numbers. ISO 6523-ICD uses International Code Designators from the ISO identification system, allowing organization-based (not geographically-based) authorities. Local (AFI values 48-51) permits proprietary non-standard addressing schemes to coexist safely with OSI addresses.

Each format is designed to allow organizations already known by an existing numbering scheme (a country code, a phone number, a telex code, or an organization code) to become an NSAP addressing authority. This flexibility means NSAP addresses can be allocated from real-world numbering authorities without creating new global registries.
sections.eli5: You can build an address using a phone number, a country code, a telex number, an organization code, or your own private scheme—whatever makes sense in your area.

sections.title: Binary and Decimal Representations
sections.content:
RFC 941 defines two concrete syntaxes (concrete encodings) for NSAP addresses: binary and decimal. The binary concrete syntax represents an AFI and decimal IDI using semi-octets (4 bits per digit, value 0000-1001), pads the IDI to its maximum length with leading zeros, represents a decimal DSP the same way, and represents a binary DSP directly as octets. The maximum length is 20 octets.

The decimal concrete syntax represents the AFI and padded IDI directly as decimal digits, represents a decimal DSP as decimal digits, and uses a table-based encoding to represent binary DSPs as five-digit groups. The maximum length is 40 decimal digits.

Additionally, a hexadecimal reference publication format (HRPF) represents binary concrete syntax with a leading solidus (/) followed by up to 40 hexadecimal digits. This allows readable representation of addresses in documentation and directories while preserving all semantic content.
sections.eli5: An address can be written as a string of binary bytes (for computers), decimal numbers (also for computers), or hex numbers after a slash (for humans to read and type).
